transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I’ve been carrying around this heavy fear and guilt. I feel tense most of the day, like something else is about to go wrong, and I keep blaming myself for not stopping what happened. I can’t really shake it.
Can you tell me what 'what happened' refers to—was there a specific event or situation that triggered these feelings?
I’m not really sure how to explain it. There isn’t one specific event I can point to right now—I just know I’ve been feeling this way.
How long have you been feeling this way—days, weeks, or longer?
About four months now. It started after my husband fell while repairing the porch.
When your husband fell, was he seriously injured or was there a moment you feared he might die or be seriously hurt?
I’m not sure. I mean, it was upsetting, but I don’t really know how badly he was hurt at the time.
Over these past four months, have you also noticed a persistent low or sad mood, or a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?
I haven’t really noticed feeling persistently sad, no. I’m still interested in the things I usually enjoy.

Is your worry mainly about your husband's fall and its aftermath, or do you also find yourself excessively worrying about other things—like work, finances, or other family matters—that aren't related to that event?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself worrying a lot about other things like that.
Along with the worry and tension, have you noticed things like feeling restless or on edge, tiring easily, having trouble concentrating, being irritable, muscle tension, or trouble sleeping?

Mostly trouble sleeping. I lie awake for an hour or two most nights, replaying what happened. And when I do get to sleep, I wake up at little sounds in the house, or from dreams where I hear him hit the ground again.
Have you found yourself avoiding places, activities, or reminders connected to your husband's fall—like the porch or watching him do repairs—because they bring back distressing memories?
Yeah. I’ve started turning down jobs with raised porches or second-story decks. And at home, I find reasons not to talk about the repair or even look at the spot where it happened.
Aside from the dreams, do you ever have sudden, vivid memories or flashbacks of the fall intruding into your mind during the day, even when you're not trying to think about it?
Yes. Sometimes I’ll be measuring a railing, or even just hear a ladder scrape, and suddenly I can see him falling like it’s right in front of me again. My stomach drops and my hands get shaky.
Do you know now, looking back, whether your husband was seriously injured from that fall—broken bones, a head injury, or anything that could have been life-threatening?
I’m not really sure. I know he fell, but I don’t know what injuries he had or how serious they were.
In the moment you saw him fall, did you think he might have been killed or seriously hurt?
I don’t know. It happened so fast—I just saw him go down, and I wasn’t thinking clearly enough to know how bad it was.
Did your husband need to go to the hospital or receive medical treatment for his injuries after the fall, and if so, do you know what that treatment was for?
I honestly don’t know. I wasn’t told whether he went to the hospital or what treatment he might have had.
When you actually saw him fall, did he appear seriously hurt at that moment—for example, was he unconscious, bleeding, or unable to move—or did he seem to be okay?
I can’t really say. I saw him fall, but I don’t remember noticing whether he was bleeding, unconscious, or able to move. It was all too quick.
Can you tell me approximately how far your husband fell—for example, from what height or off what part of the porch—so I can get a sense of how serious the fall itself was?
I’m not sure how far it was. I just remember seeing him fall from the porch, but I couldn’t tell you the height or exactly where he went over.
Did anyone—like a doctor, family member, or your husband himself—later tell you what injuries he actually had from the fall?
No. Nobody ever told me what injuries he had. I just didn’t get that information.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient developed a cluster of symptoms beginning ~4 months after witnessing her husband's fall from a porch, including intrusive memories/flashbacks with physiological reactivity, recurrent nightmares, avoidance of trauma-related cues (declining jobs with raised porches, avoiding the repair site/conversation), hyperarousal manifesting as sleep disturbance and exaggerated startle to nighttime sounds, and persistent negative emotional state (fear, guilt, tension) since the event. Mood was not persistently depressed and worry was not generalized beyond the trauma, arguing against MDD or GAD. The full symptom pattern (re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in mood, hyperarousal) is most consistent with PTSD rather than a nonspecific adjustment reaction.
